catalog_quote: [Benaissa 1979:96-97, sec. 4 'Los fonemas suprasegmentales'] El acento en sáliba no es predecible, lo que lo hace fonémico. Puede hallarse en cualquier sílaba dentro de un grupo acentual. Todas las sílabas cuyo núcleo está formado por una serie idéntica de dos vocales son acentuadas y se caracterizan todas ellas además, por una ligera prolongación de su sonido. Ejemplos: /wahamá/ 'huyeron' /wáhama/ '¿huyeron?' /núgu/ 'árboles' /nugúu/ 'árbol'. El tono es predecible con base en el acento, coincidiendo el tono alto con la sílaba acentuada. Si la palabra es esdrújula, por ejemplo, el tono desciende desde la sílaba que la sigue a la acentuada hasta la última sílaba en la cual el tono es remarcadamente bajo. En general, las sílabas que la preceden a la acentuada llevan un tono medio que crece con el acento y baja inmediatamente después, si la sílaba acentuada no es la final en la palabra. [Benaissa 1979:90, sec. 1 'El grupo acentual'] En sáliba, la palabra fonológica o grupo acentual puede estar constituido de dos a seis sílabas que llevan un acento fonético primario y están delimitadas por pausas que las preceden y las siguen. [Morse & Frank 1997:30] La palabra fonológica es de dos a seis sílabas y tiene un acento primario fonémico. El acento es contrastivo. [Estrada Ramírez 2000:683] Hasta el momento sólo se ha determinado que no es fijo, es distintivo.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: [Morse & Frank 1997:30-31] La forma canónica de la sílaba es (C)V(ʔ), donde la segunda consonante solamente puede ser la oclusiva glotal. La palabra fonológica es de dos a seis sílabas y tiene un acento primario fonémico. El acento es contrastivo. El tono alto coincide con la sílaba acentuada. Las sílabas anteriores a la sílaba acentuada tienden a tener tono medio y el tono desciende después de la sílaba acentuada. (Véase Benaissa 1979:90, 96-7.) [Estrada Ramírez 2000:683] 10.1.2. El acento. Al parecer, en sáliba el acento tiene valor fonológico. Hasta el momento sólo se ha determinado que no es fijo, es distintivo. [...] Algunos ejemplos del valor fonológico del acento son: /ˈdea/ 'carne' /deˈa/ 'blanco'; /ˈcaha/ 'mi chinchorro' /caˈha/ 'mi boca'; /ˈikʷe/ 'payarín' (cierto pez); /iˈkʷe/ 'él come'
new_statements.translation: [Morse & Frank] The canonical syllable shape is (C)V(ʔ), where the second consonant can only be the glottal stop. The phonological word has two to six syllables and carries one phonemic primary accent. Accent is contrastive. High pitch coincides with the accented syllable. Syllables before the accented syllable tend to have mid pitch, and pitch falls after the accented syllable. (See Benaissa 1979:90, 96-7.) [Estrada Ramírez] 10.1.2. Accent. Apparently, accent in Sáliba has phonological value. So far it has only been determined that it is not fixed; it is distinctive. [...] Some examples of the phonological value of accent are: /ˈdea/ 'meat' vs /deˈa/ 'white'; /ˈcaha/ 'my hammock' vs /caˈha/ 'my mouth'; /ˈikʷe/ 'payarín (a fish)' vs /iˈkʷe/ 'he eats'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Each phonological word (2-6 syllables) bears one primary accent whose position is not predictable: accent is phonemic/contrastive (minimal pairs differing only in accent position), realized with high pitch on the accented syllable, mid pitch before it and falling pitch after it. Accent also alternates morphologically (e.g. sg. upá-he vs pl. úpa-he; indicative -á accented vs interrogative -a unaccented).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; Morse & Frank speak only of 'un acento primario fonémico' per word.
new_statements.exceptions: Estrada Ramírez 2000 explicitly flags the topic as under-studied ('no se ha trabajado suficientemente.. será tema de una próxima investigación'). Morse & Frank: demonstratives pi-/hi- apparently cannot bear accent (fn. 23, p. 39); interrogative -a is unaccented (pp. 47-48); some singular/plural pairs differ only in accent (p. 33).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word ('la palabra fonológica.. tiene un acento primario fonémico'); pitch contour described over the word; examples are citation forms and inflected words.
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe Colombian Sáliba of Casanare (Orocué area). Morse & Frank's data are mainly from Morichito (río Casanare) and the Orocué resguardos; they note two Colombian dialects (río Meta vs río Casanare) differing chiefly in /d/~/ʔd/ in one suffix. Estrada Ramírez 2000 restricts herself to the Piñalito variety of the El Duya/Paravare resguardos (Orocué, Casanare). All = Glottolog sali1298; no separate dialect glottocodes involved. Not to be confused with Austronesian Saliba (sali1295, PNG).

new_statements.quote: En sáliba existen palabras con diferente significado que se pronuncian y escriben de igual modo pero que se distinguen por el acento o quizás por el tono. Existen otras palabras que no se diferencian en su pronunciación ni en su escritura, tienen el mismo acento, pero diferente significado y en ese caso serían palabras homófonas. Es decir, podría haber dos tipos de palabras en sáliba: palabras con igual escritura que tienen diferencias acentuales o tonales y palabras homófonas. Por el momento no se puede asegurar ni lo uno ni lo otro, pues se requiere de un mayor estudio y análisis de los sonidos para estas distinciones. [p. 36] … Sonograma 30. [óxoxò]~[oxóxò], óxoxò/oxóxò, “hoja”/”aguacero”. [p. 37]
new_statements.translation: In Sáliba there are words with different meanings that are pronounced and written the same way but are distinguished by accent or perhaps by tone. There are other words that differ neither in pronunciation nor in spelling, have the same accent, but a different meaning, and in that case they would be homophones. That is, there could be two types of words in Sáliba: words with the same spelling that show accentual or tonal differences, and homophones. For the moment neither can be asserted, since a fuller study and analysis of the sounds is required for these distinctions. [p. 36] … Sonogram 30. [óxoxò]~[oxóxò], óxoxò/oxóxò, 'leaf'/'downpour'. [p. 37]

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog/existing statement (Morse & Frank 1997: contrastive phonemic primary accent, high tone on the accented syllable; Estrada Ramírez 2000: accent distinctive, not fixed). Adds instrumental evidence for one accent/pitch-distinguished pair, the accent-conditioned lengthening, the first-vowel accent in VV' sequences, and an explicit hedge that the distinction might be tonal rather than accentual. It does not give a placement rule and does not contradict anything recorded.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is stated. The paper is an instrumental study of segments; on prosody it reports (a) pairs of words with identical segments whose meaning differs by accent 'or perhaps tone', with a spectrogram showing a high pitch on the first vs. the second syllable of oxoxo 'hoja'/'aguacero' (p. 38: for 'hoja' the second [o] has low pitch, for 'aguacero' a higher pitch), while explicitly refusing to decide whether the distinction is accentual or tonal; (b) accent causes phonetic vowel lengthening (p. 25: 'vocales que sufren un alargamiento, provocado por el acento que recae sobre ellas.. esta característica de aumento de la duración vocálica es fonética'); (c) in (C)VV' sequences the first vowel is accented and the second glottalized and unaccented (pp. 29-30, 38). Taken together this is consistent with a contrastive (lexical) accent whose position is not predictable, but the authors themselves leave it open.
new_statements.exceptions: None in the sense of stress placement; the paper notes that identical-spelling pairs may instead be true homophones, and that some pairs (e.g. óxoxò/oxóxò) were only verified in two sonograms; it lists candidate pairs for future study (oxóxó/oxóxo, yénejé/yénéje, ñodaga, dodaga, chiña, itebe, jano, jwãpo).
new_statements.identity_note: Benaissa 1979 describes the Sáliba of the río Meta near Orocué and the then newly founded Morichito on the río Casanare, from 1972 fieldwork (p. 90). González Rátiva & Estrada 2008 use word lists from the Orocué and Morichito communities in Casanare, recorded in 2000. Both therefore describe the same Colombian Llanos varieties as Morse & Frank 1997 (who distinguish Meta and Casanare dialects). Neither work claims a dialect-specific accent rule.

new_statements.translation: Accent in Sáliba is not predictable, which makes it phonemic. It can be found on any syllable within an accentual group. All syllables whose nucleus is formed by an identical sequence of two vowels are accented and are, moreover, all characterized by a slight prolongation of their sound. Examples: /wahamá/ 'they fled', /wáhama/ 'did they flee?', /núgu/ 'trees', /nugúu/ 'tree'. Tone is predictable on the basis of accent, the high tone coinciding with the accented syllable. [pp. 96-97] … In Sáliba, the phonological word or accentual group may consist of two to six syllables that bear one primary phonetic accent and are delimited by pauses preceding and following them. [p. 90]

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog's existing statement (Morse & Frank 1997, who cite Benaissa 1979:90, 96-7, and Estrada Ramírez 2000): contrastive, unpredictable accent with high tone on the accented syllable. Adds the domain (2-6 syllable accentual group, one primary accent), the generalization that long-vowel syllables are always accented, and the tone contour rule. This is the primary source behind the existing statement. Note: the listed open_url (sil.org search page) was not used; the file held by the project came from an Internet Archive copy of the SIL reapdata PDF recorded
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary accent per phonological word (accentual group of 2-6 syllables); its position is not predictable and is phonemic, it may fall on any syllable (minimal pairs wahamá/wáhama, núgu/nugúu). Syllables with a long (identical two-vowel) nucleus are always accented and slightly lengthened. Tone is derived from accent: high on the accented syllable, mid on preceding syllables, falling afterwards to a markedly low final if the accent is not final (pp. 96-97); tone is further modified by sentence and discourse context (p. 97).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; the description is of one primary accent per accentual group.
new_statements.exceptions: Long-vowel (VV identical) syllables are always accented; no other exceptions given.
new_statements.identity_note: Benaissa 1979 describes the Sáliba of the río Meta near Orocué and the then newly founded Morichito on the río Casanare, from 1972 fieldwork (p. 90). Both therefore describe the same Colombian Llanos varieties as Morse & Frank 1997 (who distinguish Meta and Casanare dialects). Neither work claims a dialect-specific accent rule.
